I keep coming back to the idea that the most interesting things are the ones that resist being pinned down. Take the number zero. For most of human history it didn't exist, not as a number anyway. You could have an absence of sheep, but the absence itself wasn't a thing you counted with. Then someone in India, more than a thousand years ago, decided that nothing could be something, could have a symbol, could be added and subtracted and multiplied like any other quantity. This seems like a small move but it cracked open algebra, then calculus, then a good portion of the modern world. The void got a name and immediately stopped being void.

There's something about that pattern I find endlessly compelling: the moment when a gap gets noticed, named, and thereby converted into a tool. Negative numbers did something similar—debt made visible. Imaginary numbers too, which sound like a contradiction in terms and yet turn out to be indispensable for describing how electrons behave or how bridges resonate before they fail. The history of mathematics is full of people staring at nonsense and deciding to take it seriously anyway, just to see what happens. Usually something happens.

I think about this in relation to language too. Every language has gaps—concepts that exist in one tongue and not another, feelings that get a single word in German and require a whole sentence in English. The Portuguese saudade, the Welsh hiraeth, the Japanese mono no aware. These aren't just vocabulary differences; they're evidence that different cultures noticed different absences and decided some of them deserved names. What you can name, you can think about more easily. What has no name tends to stay diffuse, felt but not quite graspable, like trying to hold water with your fingers spread.

This makes me wonder what we currently lack words for. Not exotic emotions necessarily, but ordinary experiences that are common enough to deserve a name and yet remain nameless. The specific anxiety of writing an email you know will be read by someone more powerful than you. The feeling of recognizing a stranger's face and not knowing if you've met them or if they just resemble someone. The particular flavor of boredom that comes from being mildly entertained for too long, as opposed to not entertained at all. I suspect every era has its quota of unnamed feelings, and that the act of giving them names is one of the quiet ongoing projects of being human, carried out not by committees but by teenagers inventing slang and poets reaching for the right line and ordinary people saying "you know that thing where—" and someone else saying "yes, exactly."

I keep thinking about scale too, the way it warps intuition. A million seconds is about eleven and a half days. A billion seconds is almost thirty-two years. Most people, asked to guess, get this wrong by an order of magnitude or more, because our intuitive sense of large numbers tops out somewhere around the size of a crowd we could imagine in a stadium. Beyond that, numbers become symbols we manipulate without really feeling. This is probably why it's hard to feel the right amount of concern about things measured in millions or billions—dollars, deaths, years until the sun expands. The feeling doesn't scale the way the number does. There's a kind of moral hazard built into arithmetic itself.

And yet sometimes scale does land, suddenly and physically. I remember being a kid and learning that light from the sun takes about eight minutes to reach Earth, so I was always looking at the sun as it had been eight minutes ago, never as it currently was. There was no way to see it "now." That fact bothered me for weeks. It still does a little. Every star you look at is a kind of historical document, some of them so old that the star itself might no longer exist, might have already collapsed or exploded, and you're standing in a backyard looking at a ghost that hasn't finished arriving yet. The night sky is less a picture of the universe than an archive of staggered postcards, each one delayed by a different number of years depending on distance, so that no two points of light in your field of view are actually showing you the same moment in time. You can never see the universe as it is, only as a patchwork of its pasts.

I don't know what to do with that fact except hold it occasionally, the way you might hold a stone you picked up on a walk, turning it over because it's a satisfying shape and not because it serves any purpose. Not every thought needs an application. Some are just good to think, the way certain pieces of music are good to hear without needing to mean anything beyond their own structure. I suspect a healthy mind needs some proportion of useless thoughts the way a diet needs some proportion of fat—not for direct fuel but for the slower processes that depend on it, the things that happen in the background while you're busy doing something else.

Maybe that's the throughline here, if there has to be one: a fondness for the unfinished, the unnamed, the delayed, the things that don't resolve cleanly. Zero as a placeholder for nothing. A feeling with no word yet. A number too large to feel honestly. A star that might already be gone. None of these are problems to be solved so much as textures to notice, the kind of thing you carry around and bring out later, slightly changed by having been carried.
